papers.title: From Item Scores to Semantic Tokens: Test-Time Collaborative Adaptation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Xiongfeng Shan, Xing Tang, Hanchong Chen, Fuyuan Lyu, Lingjie Li, Jingyan Jiang, Duguang Liu, Xiuqiang He
papers.abstract: Generative recommenders using semantic identifiers predict items through successive token decisions, but beam search may irreversibly prune promising item paths. This limitation is particularly consequential when a few recent interactions signal an emerging interest while earlier behavior favors established preferences. Yet an independently trained discriminative recommender may rank the same items highly from the same interaction history. Such complementary scores are available at test time, offering a way to adapt a frozen generator without retraining either model. The challenge is to use these scores before pruning: combining completed recommendation lists cannot alter earlier beam decisions, while scores over complete items cannot directly inform choices among semantic prefixes shared by multiple items. We propose \textbf{T}est-Time \textbf{C}ollaborative \textbf{B}eam \textbf{S}earch \textbf{A}daptation (\textbf{TCBSA}), a training-free method that incorporates collaborative information into semantic decoding. TCBSA transforms discriminative score margins into potentials over shared semantic edges and uses a confidence gate to regulate their contributions to cumulative path scores before beam selection. We establish a sufficient condition for target prefix survival under global beam competition and bound score perturbations under low discriminative confidence. Full-catalog experiments show consistent improvements over strong baselines across datasets and different generative and discriminative recommenders. Analyses of emerging interests and decoding behavior demonstrate gains in recommendation accuracy and target path survival, while targeted interventions support the contribution of shared prefix corrections. TCBSA also offers a favorable balance between recommendation accuracy and inference latency compared with simply widening the native beam.
papers.summary: In generative recommendation with semantic IDs, the model writes an item's code one token at a time, and beam search keeps only the highest-scoring prefixes at each step. Once a prefix is pruned, every item beneath it can never be generated. The problem is sharpest when a user has just developed a new interest that shows up in only one or two recent interactions. This paper proposes TCBSA (test-time collaborative beam search adaptation), which ==turns a scoring model's item scores into bonuses on code prefixes before every pruning step==. The scoring model scores the whole catalog and keeps the top few hundred items; each item's margin above the cutoff is spread over every step of its code. Before each beam search ranking step, these bonuses are added to the path's cumulative score. Neither model is retrained. Added to TIGER, it raises NDCG@10 by a relative 4.9% to 30.4%, depending on the public dataset. With a narrower beam, it is also more accurate and faster than TIGER with a wider beam.

papers.title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
papers.authors: Yanshuo Chen, Chenxi Liu, Reza Shirkavand, Heng Huang
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.
papers.summary: When an LLM is quantized after training to very low bit widths, common solvers such as GPTQ decide block by block which codebook value each group of weights takes. Once a block is fixed it never changes, and near-tied alternatives are dropped. This paper proposes MPQ (message-passing quantization), which ==keeps probabilities over each block's candidate values and commits only at the end==. It alternates between two steps. One uses the layer's output error to estimate each block's weights as continuous values along with how reliable that estimate is. The other gives each candidate a probability: candidates closer to the estimate score higher, and the less reliable the estimate, the more even the probabilities. After a few rounds each block takes its most probable value, and blockwise coordinate descent polishes the result. On Llama, Qwen and Mistral models it improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with larger gains at lower bit widths. With Llama-3-8B at 2 bits, its perplexity is about 11.6, against 12.76 for the baseline.
